Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

vignette:
The attack came on a Tuesday morning during a community interfaith breakfast. Margaret, then forty-one, had been a hospital chaplain for six years, and she was standing near the buffet table when a man in a maintenance vest pulled a firearm from a tool bag. She remembers the sound—not the shots themselves, but the wet, percussive thud of bodies hitting the tile floor. What she cannot do is put those moments in order. The memories arrive as a complete sensory flood: the smell of scorched coffee and cordite, the feel of someone’s elbow driving into her ribs as the crowd surged, the sight of a woman’s grey stockinged foot twitching beside an overturned fruit platter. These images feel more real than anything that has happened since. She has come to believe that her reactions that morning—freezing against the wall, unable to move or speak, still clutching a paper napkin long after the police arrived—prove she is a lousy coper. A person who was stronger, she is certain, would have run, would have helped, would have done something useful.

In the months that followed, Margaret found herself unable to step into the hospital chapel. The institutional failure she now sees everywhere—the security guard who had been on a smoke break, the locked side exit that should have been an emergency route—has reshaped her view of every building she enters. She avoids people in uniform now, particularly security personnel and police officers, crossing the street when she sees a patrol car. This has made her commute to work treacherous, since the hospital has a police substation in its lobby. She has also started skipping meals. It began as a practical decision—she felt too nauseated to eat during her shifts—but it has become a strategy she relies on. When her stomach is empty, she tells herself, she feels lighter, more alert, better able to detect the signs she might otherwise miss. She watches other people constantly, scanning faces and hands, and she always chooses a seat with her back to a wall and a clear line to an exit. Unexpected sounds—a dropped metal tray in the hospital kitchen, a car backfiring in the parking lot—send her heart into her throat and make her vision tunnel.

The connection between what she remembers and how she behaves has tightened into a loop she cannot break. A memory surge—the full sensory reliving of that breakfast room—leaves her convinced that the world is a dangerous place, and that conviction drives her to watch others even more closely. The more she watches, the more she notices people who seem agitated or who move unpredictably, and each such observation feels like confirmation that danger is imminent, which sends her back to the memory. She has begun performing mental rituals: before she enters any room, she counts the exits three times in a specific sequence, and if she does it wrong she starts over, because she has come to believe that getting the count right might prevent something bad from happening again. She knows, intellectually, that this makes no sense, but the alternative—stopping—feels like inviting disaster.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment of positive emotion. At a colleague’s retirement party, someone told a joke and Margaret felt herself beginning to laugh. The feeling was so unfamiliar and so frightening—she had the immediate sense that if she let herself feel good, she would be caught off guard, vulnerable—that she excused herself to the restroom and stood trembling over the sink. She was confused by her own reaction. She has started to wonder whether she will ever feel safe again, and she is terrified that the answer might be no. She hopes, more than anything, to return to the work she loved, but she cannot imagine how to get there from here.
